summary: Extends IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration so an address can use randomly generated, changing identifiers instead of one based on a hardware address. This makes it harder to track a device by its address. It is on the standards track. It was replaced by RFC 4941.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 addresses normally end with a number taken from the network card, and that number never changes. This RFC lets a device make up a random ending instead, and swap it for a new one every day or so, so an observer cannot tell that two different addresses belong to the same machine.

questions: how to stop ipv6 address tracking
how do ipv6 privacy extensions work
why do ipv6 addresses track devices
subtitle: Generating temporary IPv6 addresses so a device cannot be followed around the network by its address.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 address built the usual way ends in an interface identifier derived from the network card's hardware address, so it stays the same wherever the device goes. Anyone watching the network can then match addresses across sessions and follow the device.
tldr.mechanism: The extension adds a randomized interface identifier, generated from an MD5 hash of a history value and the hardware identifier. The node builds temporary global-scope addresses from it, and retires them on a schedule so no single address lives long.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3041 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 4941.

today: RFC 3041 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 4941, which updated the same extension.

sections.title: What the Extension Changes
sections.content:
Nodes use IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration to generate addresses without needing a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol server. Addresses are formed by combining network prefixes with an interface identifier. On interfaces that contain embedded IEEE Identifiers, that is, link-layer MAC addresses, the interface identifier is typically derived from the IEEE identifier. On other interface types the interface identifier is generated through other means, for example by random number generation.

This document describes an extension to IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration for interfaces whose interface identifier is derived from an IEEE identifier. Use of the extension causes nodes to generate global-scope addresses from interface identifiers that change over time, even in cases where the interface contains an embedded IEEE identifier. Changing the interface identifier, and the global-scope addresses generated from it, makes it more difficult for eavesdroppers and other information collectors to identify when different addresses used in different transactions actually correspond to the same node.

The focus is on addresses derived from IEEE identifiers, because the concern addressed here exists only where the interface identifier is globally unique and does not change. The rest of the document assumes IEEE identifiers are in use, but the techniques described may also apply to interfaces with other types of globally unique or persistent identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: The change is small but pointed: the last part of the address, which normally comes from the network card, can instead be a number the device makes up and replaces regularly.

sections.title: The Tracking Problem
sections.content:
The use of a non-changing interface identifier to form addresses is a specific instance of the more general case where a constant identifier is reused over an extended period and in multiple independent activities. Anytime the same identifier is used in multiple contexts, it becomes possible to use it to correlate seemingly unrelated activity. For example, a network sniffer placed on a link across which all traffic to and from a particular host crosses could keep track of which destinations a node communicated with and at what times.

The document compares this with IPv4 practice. In corporations and campuses, addresses are often statically assigned and change infrequently; sites moving to dynamic allocation through DHCP still often receive the same address back, so clients end up using the same address for weeks to months. Home users on dialup lines are assigned temporary addresses each time they connect, so for them an address does not reliably identify a device over more than a few minutes. Always-on connections such as cable modems, ISDN and DSL leave a home using the same address for extended periods. The RFC also notes that the network prefix portion of an address is itself a constant identifier that identifies the topological location of the nodes behind it.

IPv6 adds a new problem. Because an address is divided into a distinct topology portion and an interface identifier portion, a fixed part of the address can hold an identifier that stays constant even when the topology portion changes. For a mobile device the address changes as it moves, but the interface identifier inside it remains the same when it is derived from an IEEE identifier, so it can be used to track the movement and usage of a particular machine. A server that logs usage information together with source addresses is also recording the interface identifier, so any technique that correlates activity by address works just as well on the interface identifier.

The proposed way out is to change the interface identifier over time and generate new addresses from it for some address scopes, so it is harder to look at addresses in independent transactions and identify which ones correspond to the same node.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 home users on dialup already got a new address every time they connected. IPv6 devices on cable or DSL keep the same hardware-derived tail everywhere they go, so an observer can stitch their sessions together.

sections.title: Generating Randomized Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
Each interface maintains an associated randomized interface identifier. When temporary addresses are generated, the current value of that identifier is used, and the same identifier can be used to generate more than one temporary address.

The document describes two approaches. The first assumes stable storage that can record state history across system restarts. The algorithm uses a 64-bit history value. The very first time the system boots, a random value is generated using techniques that help ensure the initial value is hard to guess. Whenever a new interface identifier is needed, the history value from the previous iteration is taken and the interface identifier generated as described in the IPv6 addressing architecture is appended to it. The MD5 message digest is computed over the result. The left-most 64 bits of the digest become the new interface identifier, with bit 6, where the left-most bit is numbered 0, set to zero, which marks the identifier as having local significance only. The rightmost 64 bits of the same digest are saved in stable storage as the history value for the next iteration.

The RFC explains the reason for the history value. Generating truly random numbers can be tricky, and a history scheme avoids the case where two nodes generate the same randomized identifier, both detect it, and then proceed to generate identical identifiers through the same flawed random number generation algorithm. Because the interface identifier, which will often be globally unique, is used in the calculation, two nodes that happen to generate the same randomized identifier should generate different ones on the next attempt.

MD5 was chosen for convenience and because its properties were adequate to produce the desired level of randomization. IPv6 nodes are already required to implement MD5 as part of IPsec, so the code is already present. Where stable storage is unavailable, the initial history value must be generated at random; the RFC suggests using configuration information that differs from one machine to another, such as user identity, security keys or serial numbers, appended with some random data, and computing the MD5 digest as before.
sections.plainLanguage: The device keeps a secret 64-bit value in storage and feeds it, together with its hardware address, through an MD5 hash. Half of the result becomes the new address tail, and the other half becomes the input for the next round. Because the hardware address is in the input, two devices never generate the same sequence.

sections.title: Creating, Using and Rotating Temporary Addresses
sections.content:
The extension kicks in when a node processes a Router Advertisement with a Prefix Information option carrying a global-scope prefix for autoconfiguration, that is, with the A bit set. The node processes the Prefix Information Option as usual, either creating a public address or adjusting the lifetimes of existing addresses, both public and temporary; when adjusting the lifetime of an existing temporary address it only lowers the lifetimes. When a new public address is created, a new temporary address is created as well.

The temporary address takes its lifetime values from the corresponding public address. Its Valid Lifetime is the lower of the Valid Lifetime of the public address or TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME. Its Preferred Lifetime is the lower of the Preferred Lifetime of the public address or TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME minus DESYNC_FACTOR. A temporary address is created only if the calculated Preferred Lifetime is greater than REGEN_ADVANCE time units, and in particular an implementation must not create a temporary address with a zero Preferred Lifetime.

The new temporary address is made by appending the interface's current randomized interface identifier to the prefix used for the corresponding public address. If it happens to equal an address already assigned to the interface, a new randomized identifier is generated and the step repeated. Duplicate address detection is then performed on the generated address; if DAD indicates the address is already in use, a new randomized identifier is generated and the steps repeated up to 5 times, after which a system error is logged and the attempt to generate temporary addresses for that interface is given up. Because multiple temporary addresses are generated from the same randomized identifier, the RFC recommends running DAD on the first address generated from a given identifier and skipping it on subsequent ones.

When a temporary address becomes deprecated, a new one is generated. Apart from the transient period while a temporary address is being regenerated, at most one temporary address corresponding to a public address should be in a non-deprecated state at any time. To make sure a preferred temporary address is always available, a new one is generated REGEN_ADVANCE time units before its predecessor would be deprecated. The frequency of regeneration depends on how the device is used and on the concerns of the end user; the RFC expects that clients changing their address on a daily or weekly basis is likely to be sufficient to alleviate most privacy concerns, while changing addresses every few minutes may have performance implications. A new randomized interface identifier should be generated at least once every TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME minus REGEN_ADVANCE minus DESYNC_FACTOR time units, and whenever an interface connects to a new link.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time the network advertises a prefix, the device makes a public address for itself and a second, temporary address from a random tail. The temporary one is used for outgoing connections and is replaced before it expires.

sections.title: The Defined Constants
sections.content:
The RFC fixes five constants and their defaults. TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME has a default value of 1 week, and users should be able to override it. TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME has a default value of 1 day, and users should be able to override it. REGEN_ADVANCE is 5 seconds. MAX_DESYNC_FACTOR is 10 minutes, the upper bound on the desynchronisation factor. DESYNC_FACTOR is a random value within the range 0 to MAX_DESYNC_FACTOR; it is computed once at system start rather than each time it is used, and it must never be greater than TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME minus REGEN_ADVANCE.

The desynchronisation factor exists so that clients do not all replace their addresses at exactly the same moment. Each client picks a different random offset, so the replacements spread out instead of arriving together.
sections.plainLanguage: The document fixes how long a temporary address lives, how often it is replaced, and a random offset so that a fleet of devices does not all rotate at the same instant.

sections.title: Implications of Changing Interface Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC is candid about the costs. The IPv6 addressing architecture goes to some lengths to make interface identifiers globally unique where it is easy to do so, and during the IPng discussions of the GSE proposal it was felt that keeping interface identifiers globally unique in practice might prove useful to future transport protocols. Using the algorithms in this document may complicate providing such a future flexibility.

Protecting individual privacy and effectively maintaining and debugging a network can conflict with each other. Having clients use addresses that change over time makes it harder to track down and isolate operational problems: when looking at packet traces it becomes more difficult to tell whether behaviour comes from a single errant machine or from a number of them.

Some servers refuse to grant access to clients for which no DNS name exists, by performing a DNS PTR query and then an A query to check that the name maps back into the address being used. Clients not properly registered in the DNS may therefore be unable to access some services. The RFC notes that a node's DNS name, if it does not change, serves as a constant identifier in any case, and that wide deployment of this extension could challenge the practice of inverse-DNS-based authentication, which has little validity but is widely implemented. To meet server challenges, nodes could register temporary addresses in the DNS using random names, for example a string version of the random address itself.

Because these extensions may complicate debugging, it may be site policy that temporary addresses should not be used, and implementations may provide a method for a trusted administrator to override their use.
sections.plainLanguage: Rotating addresses makes life harder for network debugging, and servers that check DNS names may refuse the connections. An administrator can therefore switch the feature off.

items.title: TEMP_VALID_LIFETIME
items.text: Default 1 week. How long a temporary address stays valid.

items.title: TEMP_PREFERRED_LIFETIME
items.text: Default 1 day. How long a temporary address is preferred for new connections.

items.title: REGEN_ADVANCE
items.text: 5 seconds. How early the replacement address is created.

items.title: MAX_DESYNC_FACTOR
items.text: 10 minutes. Upper bound on the random offset that staggers clients.

data.title: The four steps of the algorithm
data.code:
1. take the history value (or a random value)
   and append the IEEE identifier
2. compute the MD5 digest over the result
3. the left-most 64 bits, with bit 6 set to zero,
   are the new interface identifier
4. the rightmost 64 bits are saved as the next
   history value
